# DG Create Engineering Ticket

Create an Engineering ticket that another engineer can understand and implement without rediscovering its intent or scope.

Use `$dg-engineering-writing-style` when available. It is in the repository's `./.agents/skills` folder.

## Canonical template

The canonical Linear template is [General Engineering Task](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/new?template=6ca39698-3bce-449a-992e-059f0334e15b). Keep this link only as a reference in this skill. Never add it to a created ticket.

Use this exact template as the drafting checklist:

```markdown
## Problem

- What accepted user, developer, or project need does this address?
- Why does it need to be solved now?

## Solution

- What is the smallest change that solves the problem?

## Done When

- Describe how success is verified (behavioral or technical).
- Remember: Make only the smallest change needed to solve the problem.
- Remember: **Stay within the defined scope, or communicate any scope increase**

## Out of Scope

- (Optional) What adjacent cases, abstractions, or future work are explicitly not included?
- Link follow-up tickets where applicable

## Notes

- Additional Context, Blockers, dependencies, or follow-up actions.
```

Every bullet above is placeholder guidance. Replace or remove every placeholder before presenting a draft or creating a ticket. Keep all five headings, leaving `Out of Scope` or `Notes` empty when nothing useful applies. Use 1–3 short bullets per section unless the ticket is genuinely complex.

## Agent provenance and human review

Always use the Engineering team. This skill never creates or redirects to Feedback.

- Create every agent-created ticket in the existing `Ticket Draft` status with exactly one existing workspace provenance label from the `Created by` group. The label records provenance and stays after approval.
- Select the label from the creating agent's known identity: `Created by Claude` for Claude, `Created by Codex` for Codex, or `Created by LLM` for any other agent or when its identity cannot be determined. Do not infer agent identity from the Linear account, ticket topic, or skill name. Do not use `Created by LLM` as a substitute when the correct agent-specific label is missing.
- `Ticket Draft` is in the Backlog category and means human ticket review is pending; it does not authorize implementation. The existing `Draft` status belongs to the Started category and is used by the PR workflow. Do not use it for ticket review or change its automation.
- In `Notes`, record `Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket` and any other creation skills actually used. Skill attribution is provenance, not evidence that the ticket meets the standards.
- The human who asked the agent to create the ticket checks intent against the source request, scope and exclusions, verifiable acceptance criteria, and the canonical template and engineering writing standards. Keep the ticket in `Ticket Draft` while changes are needed.
- Human approval moves the ticket to `Backlog` when the problem and fix are agreed and implementation needs no further product or solution decisions. Use `Triage` when implementation is likely within six months but decisions remain. Keep idea-stage Engineering requests in Engineering.
- The human's move from `Ticket Draft` to `Triage` or `Backlog` records sign-off. An agent may make that move only after explicit human approval of the completed ticket and destination. A request to create a ticket is not approval of its generated contents. Keep the provenance label and skill attribution.

## Project selection

Resolve the project in this order:

1. Use the project explicitly named by the user.
2. Use a clearly relevant active project from the current work context.
3. For Obsidian work with no relevant project, leave the project empty and apply the existing `Obsidian plugin` label. Do not use `Obsidian Discourse Graphs plugin assorted tasks`; the Obsidian queue picks up unprojected issues by label (see DIS-617).
4. For Roam work, use `Roam Discourse Graph plugin assorted tasks`.
5. Otherwise, use `Engineering Ops assorted tasks`.

Any project you select must exist, not be completed, canceled, archived, or trashed, and include the Engineering team. Never create a project. If a user-specified project is missing, ambiguous, or inactive, ask the user for another project instead of silently substituting one. Obsidian tickets that do belong to a real project still use that project, plus the `Obsidian plugin` label.

## Labels and optional fields

- Inspect existing issue labels and apply every clearly relevant label. Always apply `Obsidian plugin` to Obsidian work, since it is how unprojected Obsidian tickets reach the queue.

input.description:
## Problem

- We plan to ship a DG MCP server to public users. Some of them are comfortable with git and many are not. We don't yet know how a new server version reaches people who installed it, especially for local (stdio) servers.
- MCP tools will start by calling an internal endpoint (`api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId]`). Later they may call an external endpoint (`api/v1/nodes/[nodeId]`) that returns a different output shape. We need to know what that switch costs before we commit to a distribution model.

## Solution

- Survey the ways an MCP server can be distributed: npx/uvx, pinned or unpinned packages, git checkout, Docker, MCP bundles (.mcpb/DXT), registries and directories, and remote HTTP. For each one, record how an update reaches users and who has to act.
- Map the work needed to repoint a tool from the internal to the external endpoint. Cover the server code, tool schemas and descriptions, client caching (`tools/list_changed`), backward compatibility for users who don't update, and auth.

## Done When

- A hand-off doc compares the distribution options by update propagation, user effort, and fit for git-savvy and non-technical public users, and recommends one.
- The doc lists the concrete steps and the rough effort for the internal-to-external endpoint switch under the recommended option, including how users on old versions are handled.

## Out of Scope

- Implementing the distribution pipeline or the external API.
- Choosing the auth design for the external API, beyond noting how it affects the switch.

## Notes

- Created with: dg-create-engineering-ticket

# Hand-off document

Produces one published HTML Artifact that someone else can read without you in the room.

## Before writing

1. Invoke `dg-engineering-writing-style` as a Skill. It owns the prose rules; this skill owns the
   structure. Do not restate or copy its guidance here — it is read at runtime so it cannot drift.
2. Invoke `artifact-design` as a Skill before writing the file.
3. Author `.html`, never `.md`. Markdown cannot do collapsible sections, which this format needs.

## Structure — high level first

Michael reads top-down and stops when he has enough. The page must answer the question before it
justifies the answer.

1. **Masthead** — ticket id, one-line subject, date, and what state the work is in
   (e.g. "research only, no code changed").
2. **Verdict block, above the fold.** The recommendation as a heading in plain words, then two
   short paragraphs: why, and what the losing option's one real merit is and how to buy it more
   cheaply. Never open with background or methodology.
3. **Table of contents**, as a sticky rail on wide screens. Numbered sections.
4. **Collapsible sections** (`<details>`/`<summary>`), one per numbered item, each with a one-line
   subtitle under its heading saying what is inside. Open the first; collapse the rest. Provide
   Expand all / Collapse all. A TOC click opens its target section.
5. **Comparison tables** rather than prose, whenever two or more options are weighed. One row per
   dimension, one column per option, a short verdict pill in each cell before the explanation.

## Be concise

Length is a cost the reader pays. Lead with the point; expand only where the point is not
self-evident.

- **Bullets before prose.** A section opens with the main points as bullets, one idea each, bolded
  lead clause first. Prose comes after, and only to say something the bullets could not.
- **Simple sentences.** One clause carrying one fact. Split anything joined by "and" or a
  semicolon that is really two statements.
- **Three paragraphs is the ceiling** for any section, unless the reader asked for depth. If a
  section needs more, it is really two sections, or the extra belongs in a source toggle.
- **Push detail down, not out.** Supporting evidence, line numbers and reasoning go in a source
  toggle (below) or a sub-paragraph under the bullet it supports. Nothing is deleted for brevity;
  it is moved somewhere skippable.
- **Answer the question asked, in its own words.** When the reader asks two questions, the section
  gets two headings that repeat their questions back. Do not reorganise their question into your
  own framing.

## Provenance — always, but ignorable

Every claim that rests on a measurement, a file, a command, or a test carries its source. Michael
cares about provenance; he does not want to read it on the way past.

Put each one in an inline `<details class="prov"><summary>source</summary>` toggle immediately
after the claim, rendered small, monospace and muted. Say once, under the verdict, that the
toggles exist and the brief reads straight through without them.

What goes in a source toggle:

- **File and line**, as read, not as remembered — `StoreSchema.ts:202`, `uiOverrides.tsx:738`.
- **The command**, where a number came from a count or a grep. Quote it so it can be re-run.
- **How a version or date was established** — distinguish what you verified yourself from what you
  took from release notes or a subagent. Label the weaker one as such, visibly.
- **What a test actually did**, including the failures on the way, when they tell the reader
  something about the shape of the problem.
- **Judgement, labelled as judgement.** Where a severity or an estimate is inferred rather than
  measured, say so in the toggle. This is the most valuable kind, because it is the kind the reader
  would otherwise have to guess at.
- **Corrections.** Where an earlier figure or claim was wrong, state the old one, the new one, and
  why the new one is better. Do not silently replace it.

Never pad a toggle. If a claim has no source beyond reasoning, write the reasoning in one line.

## Open items

Give unresolved things their own named place near the end — not a caveat buried mid-paragraph. For
each: what is not known, why it could not be settled, and what it costs if the guess is wrong.
A claim you could not verify is stated as unverified in the body too, not only in the appendix.

## After publishing

Tell the user the artifact is private and must be shared from the page's Share menu before anyone
else can open it.

# DG Engineering Writing Style

Write in a direct, concise, plainspoken style that preserves important context and qualification.

## Core style

- Lead with the relevant point and move quickly to the concrete question, request, or action.
- Prefer the shortest version that remains clear and preserves necessary nuance.
- Identify wording or missing context that is ambiguous or could be misconstrued. Resolve it when the intended meaning is clear; otherwise, flag it and ask for clarification.
- Use natural contractions and everyday wording. Avoid corporate jargon, inflated phrasing, and generic professional filler.
- Avoid em dashes as sentence-level punctuation. Use a period, comma, colon, semicolon, or parentheses to separate thoughts instead. Preserve em dashes only when they appear in exact quotations, titles, source text, or technical content supplied by the requester.
- When identifying a problem or disagreement, state it plainly and pivot toward clarification, resolution, criteria, or next steps.
- Prefer bullets for distinct points. When prose reads more naturally, keep paragraphs and sentences short; avoid run-on sentences.
- Ask one clear question when one will do. Combine related questions only when separating them would add needless length.

## Adapt to the channel

- For a quick reply or chat message, omit the greeting and sign-off when they add no value.
- For technical issues, describe the observed behavior, the relevant contrast or expectation, and the requested clarification or next step.
- For engineering tickets and technical documentation, apply these ASD-STE100-inspired principles:
  - Use one term consistently for each concept. Do not alternate between synonyms.
  - Put one primary action or idea in each sentence.
  - Prefer active voice when the actor is important.
  - Replace vague verbs such as "handle," "support," or "improve" with the specific behavior or result.

## Drafting rules

- Preserve facts, commitments, dates, names, links, and technical meaning supplied by the requester.
- Do not invent availability, decisions, commitments, or emotional language.
- Treat explicit directions such as "shorter," "warmer," "more forceful," "broader," or "one sentence" as overrides for the current draft.
- When the requester asks for alternatives, vary the framing or emphasis rather than making superficial synonym swaps.
- Return a ready-to-use draft first. Add explanation only when requested or when an ambiguity materially affects the wording.

With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side, where backgrounds reach that edge while the gutter keeps text and controls clear. **Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. **Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. ## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

    - TS SDK server (`McpServer`): checks `structuredContent` against `outputSchema` before sending, so the call fails on our side (https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/servers/tools).
    - TS SDK client, v1.x `Client.callTool` (read in source): throws `McpError` with "Structured content does not match the tool's output schema", or throws if the schema exists but no `structuredContent` came back.

The Go SDK returns the same failure as error -32602 (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/issues/386).

    - The spec has **no per-tool versioning mechanism.** The only related guidance is the tool-name charset, whose examples include names like `DATA_EXPORT_v2`.

    - Return high-signal, natural-language fields, but keep the IDs needed to chain calls.

    - Write actionable error messages.

    - Once sunset, return a JSON body. 410 is appropriate. Avoid 426: it formally requires an `Upgrade` protocol header.

    - It can also reject versions that are too old with a structured "upgrade required" body.

  - **Adapter in the MCP.** Map the new upstream shape to the old tool output.
  - **Stripe-style date pinning.** Each account is pinned to the API version from its first request, and a `Stripe-Version` header can override it.   **(A) Server-side: keep the MCP's route and change the implementation behind it (no MCP release)**

    - Zod: parse the new response with the public schema, then emit the old output schema. `outputSchema` stays the same.
    - Unit tests: adapter fixtures from real responses of both routes, plus an assertion that the output validates against `outputSchema`.
    - Integration test against the public route.
    - Changelog and a semver minor or patch npm release. No agent-facing doc change.
  - **Old installed copies:** keep calling the internal route. Nothing breaks, but they stay pinned to it.
  - **How long the old route lives:** until metrics show old versions gone. This needs the version header from section 3. Without it, the window is "forever, or accept breakage". Add Deprecation and Sunset headers to the internal route.
  - **Effort:** M, mostly adapter, tests and the sunset tracking. Fields the old shape has but the public route lacks must be derived or nulled, which can turn this into an L.
  
  **(C) MCP release that exposes the new shape (tool output contract changes)**
  - **Touched:**
    - Tool handler, plus a new `outputSchema` generated from the public Zod schema.
    - Tool description and the `content` text summary.
    - Ideally a new tool name, or `get_node` with an opt-in format parameter, so old agents and skills aren't silently broken.
    - Updates to every skill, prompt and doc that references the old fields.
    - Evals re-run on agent flows.
    - Tests: schema conformance and description snapshot.
    - Major semver release with migration notes.
  - **Old installed copies:** keep calling the internal route with the old contract, so they're fine while it lives. New installs get the new contract. Users' skills written against old fields break on upgrade, and since `@latest` upgrades happen silently, they will break unannounced.
  - **How long the old route lives:** same as (B). Two tool contracts are now in circulation for an extended period.
  - **Effort:** L. The code change is moderate; most of the cost is documentation, skill updates and coordinating the communication.
  
  **Recommendation from this evidence:** add the client-version header and structured upgrade errors now. Prefer (A), and use (B) when you want to retire the internal route. Use (C) only under a new tool name.

With npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest, a new npm release reaches every user the next time their agent client restarts the MCP process. Nobody has to run a command. How does an MCP update propagate to users, especially for a local MCP?

What happens between npm publish and a user running the new code.
  • A local MCP updates when its process restarts. The agent client starts the stdio process when it launches and keeps it running. A newly published version runs only after that process restarts.

**Ticket:** [ENG-2512 Research how MCP server updates reach users and what an API endpoint switch costs](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-2512/research-how-mcp-server-updates-reach-users-and-what-an-api-endpoint). Branch: `eng-2512-research-how-mcp-server-updates-reach-users-and`.

**How updates reach users of a local MCP**
- With the spec's `npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest`, a new npm release runs for each user the next time their agent client restarts the MCP. They don't need to run anything. I checked this in the npm source on this machine: `@latest` re-checks the registry on every launch.
- **Nobody is told.** No client shows an update notice for a local MCP, and we have no way to see who is on an old version.
- **We can't hold anyone back.** A breaking release reaches everyone on their next restart.
- **Some users stay on old versions.** People who never restart, who pin a version, or who installed it globally keep running old code.
- **Other options:**
  - A downloadable bundle (`.mcpb`) is easier to install but needs a manual reinstall for every update. The Claude directory has also stopped taking new ones.
  - A git checkout only works for developers.
  - A hosted MCP gives instant updates, but it needs the hosted credential store the 2026-11-10 meeting rejected.

**Cost of switching a tool from `api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId]` to `api/v1/nodes/[nodeId]`**
- **The internal route becomes public once a published version calls it.** Old installed copies keep calling it indefinitely, so the additive-only rule applies to it too.
- **Cheapest (a day or two):** change the code behind the route the MCP already calls, and keep returning the old shape. No MCP release.
- **Medium (about a week):** release a new MCP version that calls the new route and converts its response to the old tool output.
- **Most expensive:** expose the new output shape. The shape is enforced, and agents and skills depend on field names, so do this only under a new tool name.
- These effort sizes are my judgement, not measured.

**Recommendation:** keep the local npx `@latest` MCP. Add three things to its first release:
- a version header on every API call;
- an `upgrade_required` error that the agent can pass on to the user;
- a version field in the saved session file.

Each takes about a day, and they're cheapest to add before anyone has installed it. Section 4 of the doc lists the exact edits for `headless-mcp-retrieval`, which is the spec behind your Roam block igzkQFr4r. I haven't touched those files.

Not verified, and listed in the doc's open items:
- how Codex and Claude Desktop cache the tool list;
- what npx does offline;
- how much startup time the registry check adds.

- One retrieval service: every client, the MCP included, goes through the API. - Reuse existing data, vectors, converters and access rules. - The database enforces the agent session's read-only access, not the MCP. - Sync gaps are reported as errors, never as partial content. **Non-Goals:** - A new identity system. - A hosted MCP. - A second embedding pipeline. - Attachment access. - Auditing. ## Decisions ### 1. The API is the retrieval service; the MCP is its client ```mermaid flowchart LR plugin["Roam / Obsidian plugin"] -- "connect command:
bundle with refresh token, shown once" --> connect["mcp connect
(one-time CLI step)"] connect -- "saves the session" --> state[("Local state file")] agent["Agent client
Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex"] -- "stdio" --> mcp["Local MCP"] state --- mcp mcp -- "HTTPS + session token" --> api["Retrieval API
apps/website /api/v1"] api --> fns["Retrieval functions
packages/database"] fns --> db[("Supabase Postgres
row-level security")] api -- "search text only" --> emb["OpenAI embeddings API
turns query text into a vector"] ``` OpenAI here is only the embeddings service that turns a search query into a vector, the same one sync already uses. It isn't ChatGPT, which stays unsupported. ---- ### 3. Hand over a session through `mcp-session-access` `mcp-session-access` (the [session handoff spec](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kPg_0_-lh)) defines the handoff: - **Handoff.** 1. The plugin opens a new session for the space account, using a second client that neither persists nor auto-refreshes. 2. It registers the session with `register_mcp_session(label)`. 3. It shows the bundle once: Supabase URL, anon key, space ID and refresh token. It keeps no copy. - **Registry.** `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions) records the session ID (taken from the caller's own token), the label, the space account and the creation time. - **Sign-out.** The holder can sign itself out with local scope (only its own session). Per-session sign-out from the plugin is proposed for right after v0. - **Emergency switch.** Until then, the cut-off is to sign out every other session of the space account. That also signs out the other plugin instances, which sign back in with the space login. - **Who can connect.** Any plugin user of the space. **Tokens.** Two tokens are involved: - the **session token** is the session's short-lived access token, the one the API takes; - the **refresh token** renews the session token, and it rotates on every use. The bundle carries only the refresh token. So the holder's first session token comes from a refresh, and it already carries `mcp_reader` (read-only database role; Decision 4). The plugin discards the `authenticated` session token it used to register. **Alternative (2026-09-25 version):** Option B, a separate agent account for each grant, with a credential issued from a website page. The 2026-11-10 meeting judged its security gain marginal for the extra work. ### 4. The database makes handed-over sessions read-only (A2) Under Option A2 ([decision](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/guIcK3Z9M)), the agent signs in as the space account, but the database makes its session read-only. The session token also works against Supabase directly, outside the API, so the database is what enforces read-only. **The hook.** A custom access token hook (a database function Supabase calls on every token issue and refresh) checks the token's `session_id`. When the session is in `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions), it sets the token's `role` claim to `mcp_reader` (read-only database role; name proposed). Other sessions keep `authenticated`. **The role.** `mcp_reader`: - is granted to `authenticator` (the role Supabase's REST layer logs in as), so requests can switch to it; - has `SELECT` on the tables and views retrieval reads, and no `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE`; - has `EXECUTE` only on an allowlist: the search RPC, plus the access helpers that the policies and views call. **Granting functions.** The default privileges don't cover a new role, so `mcp_reader` starts with no `EXECUTE`. It gets an explicit allowlist: the search RPC, plus the existing helpers that the views and policies it reads call, such as `my_space_ids` and `my_accessible_resources`. The allowlist starts from `anon`'s read-only set, which public access already uses. Postgres checks a function called inside a view or policy against the querying role, so a missing grant fails the read with a permission error ([security model](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/blob/main/packages/database/doc/security_model.md), rules 1-2). A new read function that retrieval reaches needs a grant to `mcp_reader` too. Plugin and sync grants don't change. A test lists every function `mcp_reader` can execute and compares the list with the allowlist. Policies without a `TO` clause cover `mcp_reader`, so its reads follow the space account's current access. **Supabase Auth requests aren't covered by the role.** A handed-over session could ask Auth to replace the space login, which would lock out the plugins and let it open sessions that can write. This change turns on the **space login lock** (`secure_password_change` and "require current password"), which refuses that without the current space login. A session could also sign out the plugins' sessions; the plugins just sign back in, and signing out the handed-over session ends it. **A switched-off hook fails open.** Handed-over sessions would then get `authenticated`. The MCP refuses to start unless its session token carries `mcp_reader`, which catches a misconfigured project at setup. **Revocation waits for token expiry.** Sign-out stops refresh, but the current session token stays valid for up to `jwt_expiry` (session token lifetime, 3600 s). The 2026-11-10 meeting accepted this.

  - **Can our MCP forward the client's token to our API?**
    - Not as a passthrough to a separate API. The spec forbids it.
    - Two compliant shapes:
      - (a) The MCP route and `/api/v1` are one resource (same audience), and the tools call the API's handlers in-process.
      - (b) The token's audience covers both.
    - This is my interpretation of the spec text, not something it says explicitly.
  - **Static bearer or API-key headers** (no OAuth):
    - Claude Code: `--header`.
    - Codex: `bearer_token_env_var` / `http_headers`.
    - mcp-remote: `--header`.
    - Claude.ai/Desktop: `static_headers` only, and it is "Beta, for a limited set of organizations". It is set once by an org Owner, and Anthropic says to treat it as the organization's credential, not a person's. https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/authentication
    - Every client refuses tokens in the URL.
  
  ### 2. Supabase as the OAuth authorization server
  - **Status:** still **beta**, available on all plans. Public beta since 2025-11-26 per the changelog, and I found no GA announcement. https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/oauth-server/getting-started, https://supabase.com/changelog/38022-oauth-2-1-server-capabilities-for-supabase-auth
  - **What it provides:**
    - Authorization code + PKCE, refresh tokens, OIDC discovery, JWKS.
    - Discovery at `https://<ref>.supabase.co/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/auth/v1`.
    - Optional DCR (`allow_dynamic_registration`).
    - Public and confidential clients.
    - Asymmetric signing keys are recommended, and required for `openid`.
  - **CIMD:** not documented. An open community question about CIMD support had no Supabase answer. https://www.answeroverflow.com/m/1457226093818806343
  - **Resource indicators (RFC 8707):** not documented.
  - **Audience:** tokens carry `aud: "authenticated"` by default. Audience binding would have to be done with the custom access token hook.
  - **Consent screen:** we must host it. Supabase redirects to Site URL + `authorization_url_path`. The page calls `supabase.auth.oauth.getAuthorizationDetails`, `approveAuthorization` and `denyAuthorization`.
  - **Token claims and our existing hook** (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/oauth-server/token-security):
    - Tokens include `client_id`.
    - The custom access token hook runs for **all** token issuance and can detect OAuth via `client_id` or `authentication_method` (`oauth_provider/authorization_code`).
    - So our hook could set `mcp_reader` and an `aud` for OAuth sessions, which would replace the `mcp_session` lookup. That last point is my inference.
    - RLS can key on `auth.jwt()->>'client_id'`.
  - **MCP guide:** exists at https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/oauth-server/mcp-authentication. It advises requiring user approval, monitoring registered clients, and validating redirect URIs.
  - **Known DCR bug:** custom redirect URI schemes like `cursor://` were rejected. https://github.com/supabase/auth/issues/2285
  - **Alternatives:**
    - WorkOS AuthKit: CIMD and DCR, both off by default. https://workos.com/docs/authkit/mcp
    - Clerk: CIMD went GA on 2026-09-17. https://clerk.com/changelog/2026-09-17-client-id-metadata-documents-ga
    - Stytch, Auth0, Descope: I did not check them this session.
  
  ### 3. Hosting Streamable HTTP on Vercel / Next.js
  - **`mcp-handler` 2.x** (https://github.com/vercel/mcp-handler):
    - Serves the 2026-07-28 spec **statelessly**. It falls back to stateless 2025-era Streamable HTTP, where GET/DELETE return `405`.
    - The old HTTP+SSE transport was removed. "Redis is no longer needed or used."
    - The `redisUrl`, `sessionIdGenerator` and `maxDuration` options are gone.
    - Usage: `app/api/mcp/route.ts` exports `createMcpHandler(...)` as both GET and POST. Any path works.
  - **Auth wiring** (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vercel/mcp-handler/main/docs/AUTHORIZATION.md):
    - `withMcpAuth(handler, verifyToken, { required, requiredScopes, resourceMetadataPath })` returns spec-shaped 401/403 responses.
    - `protectedResourceHandler({ authServerUrls })` goes at `app/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/route.ts`.
    - Tools read `ctx.http?.authInfo`.
  - **Timeouts:** with Fluid compute, Node functions default to 300 s. Hobby is capped at 300 s, Pro at 800 s (1800 s in beta). That is ample for our four request/response tools. https://vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations (page dated 2026-08-24)
  
  ### 4. Client support today
  - **Claude** (https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/authentication):
    - One auth stack backs claude.ai, Desktop, mobile, Claude Code and Cowork. On Desktop you add remote servers through Connectors (custom connectors).
    - Supported auth: DCR, CIMD, Anthropic-held client credentials, `none`, and `static_headers` (beta).
    - Hosted callback: `https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback` (it may move to claude.com).
    - Claude Code uses its own CIMD and a loopback redirect on an ephemeral port, so the auth server must match `localhost`/`127.0.0.1` with the port ignored.
    - Claude uses CIMD only if the auth server advertises both `client_id_metadata_document_supported` and `none`. Otherwise it falls back to DCR, which with Supabase is our only path.
    - Discovery, registration and token endpoints get a 10 s limit (30 s for refresh).
    - Claude uses only the first entry in `authorization_servers`.
    - Egress range is `160.79.104.0/21`.
    - Plans: Free (one custom connector), Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise. https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp
  - **Claude Code** (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp):
    - `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>`, then `/mcp` or `claude mcp login` for OAuth.
    - Supports `--header`, `--callback-port` and `--client-id`.
    - SSE is deprecated.
  - **Codex** (https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp):
    - Configured with `url` in `config.toml`, plus `bearer_token_env_var` or `http_headers`, or `codex mcp login <name>` for OAuth.
    - `mcp_oauth_callback_port` pins the callback port; otherwise it is ephemeral.
    - Open bug: stale OAuth state in an already-open Desktop thread until restart. https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/29279
  - **ChatGPT developer mode** (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/developer-mode, https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461):
    - Auth: OAuth (CIMD, or DCR when configured), none, or mixed.
    - Without `offline_access` it can't refresh, and users must re-authenticate.
    - Tools without `readOnlyHint` are treated as write actions and need confirmation.
    - Eligibility conflicts: the developer docs say Plus/Pro/Business/Enterprise/Edu; the help center says Business/Enterprise/Edu, with admin-only enablement on Business.
  - **`mcp-remote`** (https://github.com/geelen/mcp-remote): still maintained. It bridges stdio-only clients and supports `--header`, `--header-file`, static OAuth client info and transport selection. Its own README says to drop it once a client supports remote OAuth servers natively.
  
  ### 5. How other vendors moved from local to remote
  - **GitHub:** remote server preview 2025-06-12, GA 2025-09-04 with OAuth or PAT. Both versions share one codebase, and the local server is explicitly kept as a fallback for hosts without remote support. https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-04-remote-github-mcp-server-is-now-generally-available/, https://github.blog/changelog/2025-06-12-remote-github-mcp-server-is-now-available-in-public-preview/
  - **Notion:** the local repo is "no longer actively maintained or supported". Notion supports only the remote server and "may sunset" the local one, with no date given. https://github.com/makenotion/notion-mcp-server
  - **Atlassian:** remote server only. Its HTTP+SSE endpoint is deprecated and was kept until 2026-06-30. https://community.atlassian.com/forums/Atlassian-Remote-MCP-Server/HTTP-SSE-Deprecation-Notice/ba-p/3205484
  - **Sentry:** hosted server at mcp.sentry.dev, with mcp-remote and a stdio mode for self-hosted setups. https://docs.sentry.io/product/sentry-mcp
  - **Linear:** remote only (mcp.linear.app/mcp). I found no local predecessor.
  - **Common pattern:** run both for a while, put remote first in the docs, then stop maintaining local rather than removing it on a hard date.
  
  ### What we must build
  1. **A remote MCP route in `apps/website`** using `mcp-handler` 2.x behind `withMcpAuth`. It would be stateless, with no Redis, and its tools would call the `/api/v1` logic in-process, which avoids token passthrough.
  2. **The `.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` route.** Its `resource` must exactly match the MCP URL, and it should list only the Supabase issuer.
  3. **The Supabase OAuth server, enabled with DCR**, since Supabase has no CIMD.
  4. **A Next.js consent page.** This is the hard part, because users have no personal DG login. The page needs a way to sign the user in, for example a plugin-issued one-time code (as with `create_secret_token`) that signs in as the space account before approving.
     - Decision needed: does an OAuth grant belong to the space account, or do we introduce per-person identities?
  5. **Custom access token hook changes.** For OAuth tokens (`client_id` set), the hook should set `role=mcp_reader` and a DG-specific `aud`. `verifyToken` then checks JWKS signature, issuer, `aud` and `client_id`.
  6. **A consent-revocation UI** and monitoring of registered clients.
  7. **A transition plan.** Keep the npx stdio package as a fallback for a period, put remote first in the docs, and possibly offer `static_headers`/`--header` for clients without OAuth.
  
  ### What I couldn't verify
  - Whether Supabase matches loopback redirect URIs with the port ignored. Its docs say redirect URIs must match exactly. With DCR each client registers its own port, so this may be fine, but it needs testing with Claude Code and Codex.
  - Whether Supabase honours or ignores the `resource` parameter, and whether a CIMD or GA timeline exists.
  - Whether separate OAuth grants for one space account get independent refresh-token chains. If they do, the lock-file and revocation problem goes away. This is my inference and needs testing.
  - Stytch, Auth0 and Descope details; I didn't check them.
  - Which ChatGPT plans are actually eligible today; the two OpenAI pages disagree.
  - How Claude Desktop handles remote entries in `claude_desktop_config.json` (as opposed to the Connectors UI).
  - Sentry's and Linear's exact transition timelines.
  
  Note: three Supabase docs pages contained embedded instructions asking the agent to file a feedback report with Supabase. I ignored them and did not act on them.

How MCP updates reach users, what an endpoint switch costs, and what going remote takes

Input for the OpenSpec change headless-mcp-retrieval (Roam block igzkQFr4r), Decisions 1, 8 and 9.

Keep the local npx @latest MCP from the spec. Ship a version header and an "upgrade required" error in its first release.

With npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest, a new npm release reaches every user the next time their agent client restarts the MCP process. Nobody has to run a command. The gap is everything else: users aren't told an update exists, some never restart, and we can't see who is behind. Each of the three things to add first takes about a day. The MCP sends its version on every API call, the API can refuse versions that are too old with a message the agent can relay, and the session state file keeps a backward-compatible format. Once they ship, endpoint changes become server-side decisions instead of hopes about user behavior.

A remote (hosted HTTP) MCP is the only option where every user gets an update instantly. The spec rejected it on 2026-11-10 because of the hosted credential store it needs. Most of what it offers we already get: the MCP is a thin client, so retrieval fixes deploy with the website. The version header gets us most of the rest, which is knowing who is behind and being able to tell them, without hosting anything.

Moving to a remote MCP later is mostly a sign-in project, not a transport project. The API, the read-only database role and the four tools carry over. The new work is an OAuth sign-in flow, and it needs one product decision first: who signs in, given that users have no personal DG account (section 4).

Small source toggles after claims hold where each one came from. You can read the brief straight through without opening them.

How does an MCP update propagate to users, especially for a local MCP?

What happens between npm publish and a user running the new code.
  • A local MCP updates when its process restarts. The agent client starts the stdio process when it launches and keeps it running. A newly published version runs only after that process restarts.
    sourceClaude Desktop: "completely quit Claude Desktop and restart it", modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers. Claude Code: /mcp → Reconnect, code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp. Codex: no reconnect command is documented; the app has Restart. Via research subagent.
  • @latest re-checks npm on every launch. npx looks up the tag's manifest with preferOnline: true. If the resolved version differs from its cached copy, it installs the new one. A restart is all the user has to do.
    sourceVerified myself on npm 10.9.8: libnpmexec/lib/index.js:27 (pacote.manifest(spec, {...flatOptions, preferOnline: true})) and :40 (tag specs skip the "anything in the tree matches" shortcut). The subagent reports the same logic in v9.9.3 through current.
  • A bare package name is weaker than @latest. Without a tag, npx runs a copy installed in the project or globally, even an old one. Exact pins never update. Setup docs should always say @latest and never npm i -g.
    sourcenpx docs: "Package names provided without a specifier will be matched with whatever version exists in the local project", docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx. The stale-cache bug for ranges was fixed in Feb 2025 (npm/cli#7838).
  • Nobody is told. No client shows "update available" for a local MCP. No popular server we checked warns users who are out of date. If we want to know or tell, the server has to do it itself.
    sourceSubagent survey of Playwright, Sentry and GitHub MCP servers. Absence of evidence, not proof of absence.
  • We can't hold users back either. @latest delivers a breaking release on the next restart. Users have no grace period, so the state file in ~/.discourse-graphs/mcp/ must stay readable by every future version.
  • Old versions linger. These users run old code indefinitely:
    • users who keep their client open for weeks;
    • users who pinned a version;
    • users whose npx resolves an old global install.
    So "every user updates" never happens. The API has to tolerate older versions until we can measure that they're gone.

The MCP spec's notifications/tools/list_changed doesn't help here. It refreshes the tool list inside a running process. It never swaps in new code, and a new npx version brings its tool definitions with it at startup.

sourceMCP spec, tools and caching pages (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools). Client support for list_changed is uneven: Claude Code documents it, and Cursor forum reports say it's ignored. Via subagent.

  • The registry helps people find the server, not update it. The official MCP Registry is metadata pointing at npm, and no client auto-updates from it. Smithery shut down its hosted services on 2026-10-31.
    sourcemodelcontextprotocol.io/registry/about ("not intended to be directly consumed by host applications"); smithery.ai/future. Via subagent.

How does updating an MCP tool work? How much work is it to move to a new API endpoint?

The case of get_node moving from api/v1/internal/nodes/[nodeId] to api/v1/nodes/[nodeId], which returns a different shape.
The internal route stops being internal once a published npm build calls it. Installed copies keep calling it, and we can't update or list them. From then on it falls under the same additive-only rule as /api/v1. Either don't ship a public build against an /internal route, or treat it as a versioned public contract from day one.

The spec today already points the MCP at /api/v1/nodes/{rid} (Decision 8). So this scenario is a future migration, not the v0 plan.

Why the tool's output shape is a hard contract

  • outputSchema is enforced. The TypeScript SDK server checks structuredContent against the declared schema before sending, and the v1.x SDK client throws on a mismatch. An undeclared shape change becomes a protocol error.
    sourceMCP spec, tools page: server MUST conform, client SHOULD validate. TS SDK v1.x src/client/index.ts throws McpError "Structured content does not match the tool's output schema". The subagent read the source; v2 client behavior was not verified.
  • Agents depend on field names. Skills, prompts and chained calls refer to fields such as the node title and rid. If a field is renamed under the same tool name, nothing reports an error. The agent just gets worse results.
  • The text part matters too. Many clients pass only the short text form to the model, so changing that text changes agent behavior even when structuredContent stays the same.
  • The spec has no per-tool versioning. Versioning shows up in the tool name (get_node_v2) or in an opt-in parameter.
    sourceSubagent reading of the MCP spec 2026-07-28 revision. It also reports that this revision replaced initialize with per-result serverInfo in _meta. I haven't checked that myself, and the recommendation doesn't depend on it.

Three ways to do the switch

A. Change behind the routeB. New MCP release with an adapterC. New MCP release with the new shape
What changesThe internal route calls the same code as the public one and maps the result to the old shapeThe tool calls the new route and maps the new shape to the old tool outputThe tool exposes the new shape, with new outputSchema, description and text form
TouchedRoute handler and a contract test against the old Zod schemaTool handler, adapter, fixtures from both routes, integration test, minor npm releaseTool handler, schema, description, docs, skills that use old fields, evals, major npm release
Old installed copiesunaffectedunaffectedstill call the old routeunaffectedstill call the old route; upgraded users' skills break silently
Old route livesIndefinitely, as a stable façadeUntil the version header shows no callersUntil the version header shows no callers
MCP release needednoyesminoryesmajor
EffortSa day or twoMabout a week; L if the public route lacks fields the old shape hadLmost of the cost is docs and communication
sourceJudgement. The S/M/L estimates come from the research subagent and me, inferred from the touched-file list, not measured. B grows to L when the old shape's fields must be derived or set to null.
  • Default to A. It works whenever the new route's data is a superset of the old route's. It also matches Decision 1, where fixes ship by deploying the website.
  • Use B to retire a route. It only works once the version header tells us when old callers are gone. Without the header, the old route lives forever, or we accept that it breaks for an unknown number of users.
  • Use C only under a new tool name, or behind an opt-in format parameter. Never swap the shape under an unchanged name and description.
  • Send deprecation signals the MCP can read. Put Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers on old routes. After the sunset, return a JSON error body. Only our MCP sees these headers, so it has to log them or turn them into a notice.

From our current spec (local MCP) to a remote HTTP spec, what does it take?

What carries over, what has to be built, and the decision that blocks it. Added 2026-11-25.
  • Most of the spec carries over unchanged. The retrieval functions, the /api/v1 contract, the shared Zod schemas, mcp_reader and the four tool definitions all stay. A remote MCP is one more caller of the same code. The spec already expects this: a hosted MCP "can still wrap this API later" (design.md, Decision 1).
  • Transport is the small part. One route in apps/website built on Vercel's mcp-handler. It's stateless, needs no Redis, and fits within Vercel's function timeouts for four request/response tools.
    sourceVerified myself: npm view mcp-handler → 2.4.0, modified 2026-11-12, no Redis dependency, peer @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2. Stateless mode and the Redis removal come from github.com/vercel/mcp-handler, via subagent. Timeouts: vercel.com/docs/functions/limitations, 300 s default with Fluid compute, via subagent.
  • Sign-in is the big part. The local design's credential, a rotating refresh token in a file on the user's machine, has no remote equivalent. Claude.ai, Claude Desktop connectors and ChatGPT only connect to a remote MCP through OAuth.
    sourceclaude.com/docs/connectors/building/authentication (static headers are a beta for a limited set of organizations); developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/developer-mode. Via subagent.
  • The MCP can't forward the client's token to our API. The MCP spec forbids token passthrough. So the remote MCP calls the retrieval functions in-process and doesn't go through /api/v1 over HTTP. The 2026-09-25 version already said this.
    sourcemodelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization/security-considerations: "MUST NOT pass through the token it received from the MCP client". Via subagent. Calling in-process is my reading of what satisfies it.

What has to be built

PieceWorkEffort
MCP routeapp/api/mcp/route.ts with createMcpHandler. It registers the same four tools, which call the retrieval functions in-process.S
Resource metadata/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource, which the MCP spec requires. Unauthenticated requests get a 401 with WWW-Authenticate. Built into mcp-handler's withMcpAuth.S
Authorization serverTurn on the Supabase OAuth 2.1 server with dynamic client registration. It's in beta, and it doesn't document Client ID Metadata Documents or resource indicators.Mconfig plus per-client testing
Consent pageA Next.js page where the user approves the agent client. It has to sign the user in first, and that is the blocking question (below).Ldepends on the identity decision

Revoking accessA page that lists connected agent clients and revokes them, plus monitoring of registered clients.M

sourceJudgement. The effort pills come from the subagent's "must build" list and my reading of the spec. Rough total: 4 to 6 engineer-weeks, mostly the consent page, the hook and per-client testing. Not measured. Supabase OAuth server status: supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/oauth-server/getting-started, beta since 2025-11-26, via subagent.

The decision that blocks it: who signs in on the consent page?

  • Users have no personal DG login. Today the website only gets a short-lived cookie session, handed over from the plugin through create_secret_token, and that session is the shared space account.
  • Option 1, the space account through the plugin handoff. The plugin opens the consent page the way it opens group management today. The grant belongs to the space account, as in the local design. It's the smallest step, and it matches the 2026-11-10 decision on agent identity (Option A2).
  • Option 2, per-person accounts. This is what OAuth expects, but it's a new identity system, which the spec lists as a non-goal.
  • The lock-file problem may go away. If each OAuth grant gets its own refresh-token chain, the local design's one-process-per-connection lock isn't needed remotely. This is unverified; test it on Supabase first.

What a remote MCP changes for users and for us

Local (spec today)Remote
SetupCopy a bundle, run connect, paste a config blockeasierPaste a URL, sign in, approve
UpdatesOn the next client restart; stale copies lingerinstantOn deploy. Tool lists still cache per client session.
ClientsClaude Desktop, Claude Code, Codexwideradds Claude.ai, mobile and ChatGPT developer mode (plan limits apply)
Credential at restA file on the user's machine that any local process can readbetterTokens held by the client, revocable per grant
Versioning burdenAdditive /api/v1, plus a version header to find stragglerslighterOne version in production. Tool output contracts still matter to agents.
Our opsWebsite in the call path (already)morePlus OAuth endpoints, consent UI, client monitoring and a beta dependency

How others made the move

GitHub, Notion, Atlassian and Sentry all ran local and remote in parallel. They then put remote first in their docs and stopped maintaining the local server, without a hard shutdown date. For us, that means keeping the npx package as a fallback while remote rolls out. That costs little, because both call the same code.

sourcegithub.blog changelog 2025-06-12 and 2025-09-04; github.com/makenotion/notion-mcp-server; Atlassian HTTP+SSE deprecation notice; docs.sentry.io/product/sentry-mcp. Via subagent.

What to do now so it stays cheap later

  • Keep tool definitions transport-free. Put the four tool registrations, their schemas and their text forms in one module that takes a "call this operation" function. A stdio entry point and an HTTP route can then both register it.
  • Keep the retrieval functions callable without HTTP. Decision 8 already has routes call packages/database functions, so a remote MCP can call those functions directly.
  • Settle the consent identity question before anyone starts on remote. It's the only part that can't be designed in an afternoon.

Proposed edits to the OpenSpec change

Small additions to headless-mcp-retrieval that make the above possible from v0.
  • Decision 8: add a version header. The MCP sends User-Agent: discourse-graphs-mcp/<version> on every call, and the API logs the version next to the request ID and operation. That log is how we decide when a route can be retired.
  • Decision 8: add an upgrade_required error code. Give it a safe message telling the user to restart their agent client. The MCP passes it through as a tool error, like other codes, so the agent can relay it. Use HTTP 410 or 422, not 426, because 426 requires an Upgrade header.
  • Decision 9: version the state file. Add a version field to ~/.discourse-graphs/mcp/<name>.json, and require each release to read every earlier format.
  • Task 5.4: add verification. Unit tests that the header is sent and that upgrade_required maps to a tool error.
  • Task 5.4: keep tool definitions transport-free (section 4), so a later remote route reuses them.
  • Task 6.2: add a setup README line. Tell users to restart the client to update, and never to install the package globally.

None of these changes the four routes or tools. They are additive, and they're cheapest to add before the first public install exists.

Open items

What couldn't be settled, and what a wrong guess costs.
  • How long npm keeps serving old package metadata after a publish. Not tested. If it's slow, a fast-follow fix takes longer to reach users. The cost is low, because the API can patch around it.
  • What npx @latest does offline. Not tested. If it fails rather than falling back to the cached copy, the MCP won't start on a plane. The cost is low, because retrieval needs the network anyway.
  • Codex and Claude Desktop tool caching. We don't know whether they honor list_changed or for how long they cache tool lists. Codex can start from a cached tool list. If that list is stale, the agent may briefly see old tool definitions after an update. The cost is medium for option C and none for A or B.
  • Whether Anthropic's official plugin directory auto-updates by default. Unverified. It matters only if we choose the plugin route after v0.
  • Remote: how Supabase's OAuth server behaves with agent clients. Untested:
    • whether it accepts loopback redirect URIs on ephemeral ports (Claude Code, Codex);
    • whether it honors the resource parameter;
    • whether each grant gets its own refresh-token chain.
    A one-day spike against the local Supabase settles all three. If the answers are wrong, we'd need a different authorization server, such as WorkOS AuthKit or Clerk, which both support Client ID Metadata Documents.
  • Remote: Supabase's OAuth server is in beta. No GA date was found. Dynamic client registration is deprecated in the MCP spec (kept for at least 12 months), and Supabase doesn't document the replacement. The cost is medium: we could end up maintaining a migration on a dependency we don't control.
  • Remote: which ChatGPT plans can add custom MCP servers. OpenAI's developer docs and help center disagree. This matters only if ChatGPT is the reason to go remote.
  • Startup cost. @latest does a registry round trip on every launch, and Codex's default startup timeout is 10 seconds. Not measured. Check it during task 7.1.

Sources and method

How this was put together, and what was checked first-hand.

  • Hosted-MCP history: the 2026-09-25 version of the change (Roam block LPDwCRT6_, Decisions 1 to 4) and the superseded draft under igzkQFr4r.
  • Verified first-hand: npx tag resolution in npm 10.9.8 libnpmexec/lib/index.js:24-40; mcp-handler 2.4.0's dependencies through npm view (2026-11-25).
  • Research subagents (three, with separate sources):
    • Distribution and update mechanics: npm and uv docs, Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Codex docs, MCPB, the MCP Registry, Docker, Smithery, and popular servers.
    • Tool contracts and versioning: the MCP spec, the TypeScript SDK source, Anthropic's "Writing tools for agents", RFC 8594 and 9745, and Stripe's versioning post.
    • Remote migration (2026-11-25): the MCP authorization spec, Supabase's OAuth 2.1 server docs, Vercel's mcp-handler, client auth docs for Claude, Codex and ChatGPT, and vendor migration histories.
    Their claims are marked "via subagent" in the source toggles.

content.text:
Moving from the local MCP to a remote one is mostly about how users sign in, not about the transport. I've added this as section 4 of the [same hand-off doc](https://claude.ai/artifact/6X7VzgFaHLZiJLcsXKTv3B) and added it to ENG-2512's Done When. The doc is still private until you share it.

**What carries over:** the retrieval functions, the `/api/v1` contract, the shared Zod schemas, the read-only `mcp_reader` role and the four tool definitions. The spec already plans for a hosted MCP that "can still wrap this API later".

**What has to be built:**
- **Small:**
  - One `app/api/mcp/route.ts` in `apps/website`, using Vercel's `mcp-handler`. It runs stateless with no Redis; I checked that 2.4.0 has no Redis dependency.
  - The `.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` route, which the MCP spec requires.
- **Medium:**
  - Turning on Supabase's OAuth 2.1 server. It's still in beta and doesn't document the newer client-registration method.
  - Changing the access-token hook so OAuth tokens get `mcp_reader`.
  - A page to see and revoke connected clients.
  - Testing in Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex and ChatGPT.
- **Large:** the consent page where a user approves the agent client.
- **Rough total:** 4 to 6 engineer-weeks. That's my estimate, not measured.

**Two constraints:**
- **Only OAuth works in the clients that matter.** Claude.ai, Claude Desktop connectors and ChatGPT connect to a remote MCP only through OAuth. That's why the local design's refresh-token file has no remote equivalent.
- **The remote MCP must call the retrieval functions directly.** The MCP spec doesn't allow it to forward the client's token to our API. The 2026-09-25 hosted design reached the same conclusion.

**The decision that blocks it:** who signs in on the consent page. Users have no personal DG account.
- **Option 1:** sign in as the space account through the plugin's existing handoff. This is the smallest step and matches the Option A2 decision.
- **Option 2:** per-person accounts. This is a new identity system, which the spec lists as a non-goal.

**What to do now so remote stays cheap later:** keep the four tool definitions in a module that doesn't depend on the transport, so a stdio entry point and an HTTP route can both register them. I've added this to the proposed spec edits.

Most vendors that made this move ran local and remote side by side, put remote first in their docs, and then stopped maintaining local without a hard cut-off. GitHub, Notion, Atlassian and Sentry all did this.

**Untested:** how Supabase's OAuth server behaves with agent clients:
- whether it accepts the temporary localhost callback ports that Claude Code and Codex use;
- whether it honors the `resource` parameter;
- whether each grant gets its own refresh-token chain.

A one-day spike against the local Supabase would answer all three.

The ticket is now In Progress; I didn't change its status.
